US oil giant ExxonMobil is challenging EU rules requiring fossil fuel producers to help fund carbon storage infrastructure, in a legal battle that could undermine Brussels’ efforts to make the industry pay for the energy transition.

Oil and gas giant ExxonMobil is suing the European Commission over EU rules requiring fossil fuel producers to contribute to carbon storage targets, according to an official Commission document seen by Euronews.

Three companies belonging to the ExxonMobil group have filed a notice of arbitration under the Energy Charter Treaty (ECT), using rules established by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law, the document reveals.

The ECT is a post-Cold War international agreement originally designed to protect investments in unstable, formerly communist states. It has since become controversial because it allows energy companies to sue governments over measures that could harm their expected profits.

The companies – ExxonMobil Petroleum & Chemical, incorporated in Belgium, ExxonMobil Luxembourg and ExxonMobil Netherlands – are challenging provisions of the EU's Net Zero Industry Act (NZIA) obligations on carbon storage.

"The companies challenge the carbon storage infrastructure element of the regulation, which sets a Union-level objective of reaching a CO₂ injection capacity of at least 50 million tonnes per annum by 2030 and requires contribution of authorised oil and gas producers," the letter says.

ExxonMobil argues that the EU's stringent climate requirements are impossible to meet because of lengthy permitting procedures and high costs. Although the document does not specify when the challenge was launched, previous reports suggest it was filed in July.

Under the NZIA, authorised oil and gas producers must contribute to the EU's target of achieving 50 million tonnes of annual CO₂ injection capacity by December 31, 2030. The rules reflect the principle that companies extracting fossil fuels should help build the infrastructure needed to manage carbon emissions.

A challenge to the polluter-pays logic?

The legal confrontation could test Brussels' ability to make fossil fuel companies pay for the energy transition, just as the Commission is already delaying its proposal for new rules on the CO₂ transport infrastructure and markets, which was slated for the third quarter of the year.

The NZIA obligations are further specified in two EU measures — one establishing the production threshold determining which companies are covered and another decision setting the required injection-capacity contributions.

Companies producing less than 610,000 tonnes of oil equivalent or accounting for less than 5% of total EU production are exempt. In all, 44 major oil and gas producers are subject to the rules.

ExxonMobil alleges that the EU has breached provisions of the ECT relating to fair and equitable treatment, non-discrimination and the protection of investments against expropriation.

The companies have announced that they intend to seek provisional measures to suspend the obligation to inject CO₂ underground as it applies to their affected subsidiaries, according to the letter.

The case raises questions about how far the EU can go in making established fossil fuel producers financially responsible for infrastructure needed for the energy transition.

Brussels has presented the 50-million-tonne target as a way to accelerate the development of carbon capture and storage, a technology considered important for cutting emissions in hard-to-abate industrial sectors, albeit criticised for its "expensive" and "unproven" technology by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis and.

The EU rules place a direct responsibility on oil and gas producers instead of leaving the development of carbon storage capacity entirely to public funding or voluntary private investment.

As a result, the dispute could have implications beyond ExxonMobil's individual investments, especially if the companies succeed in challenging the legal basis or implementation of the contribution mechanism.

Brussels is still analysing the notice and preparing its response, according to the document.

Details of the compensation sought by ExxonMobil or the financial exposure facing the EU aren't provided.

The European Commission told Euronews it does not comment on ongoing legal cases.

Commission hails new carbon capture project

The legal challenge comes as the Commission continues to champion carbon capture and storage as a key part of Europe's climate strategy.

In September, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra hailed the launch of Europe's largest carbon capture facility in the Netherlands.

The new Yara facility in Sluiskil is meant to capture 800,000 tons of carbon dioxide every year, cutting the plant's emissions by 25%. The carbon will be turned into liquid, put on ships and buried deep under the seabed in Norway through the Northern Lights project.

Commissioner Hoekstra conceded that carbon capture and storage "isn’t a silver bullet solution to the climate crisis" but argues it could become a vital part of the solution mix, especially for energy-intensive sectors like steel, cement and aluminum.

"We simply cannot afford to leave any part of the solution space untapped. This is a practical climate solution that cuts emissions while keeping our industrial base strong," the Dutch Commissioner said from Yara's facility on 7 September.

Speaking from Sluiskil, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said that a few years ago, storing carbon underground was nearly impossible for skeptics.

"Now it’s a reality. The project shows that carbon capture and storage works and can be carried out across national borders. Norwegian expertise and infrastructure are being used to reduce greenhouse gas emissions far beyond Norway’s own borders and are playing an important role in Europe's green transition," said Støre.

Model projections estimate the EU will need around 250 million tonnes of annual storage capacity to reach its 2040 climate target of a 90% reduction in net emissions.

Most prominent projects — such as Porthos and Aramis (Netherlands) and Greensand and Bifrost (Denmark) — are clustered around the North Sea.

Major hurdles remain

Bergur Rasmussen, a former Danish MEP who now heads the advocacy group CCS Europe, described the EU's 2030 target of 50 million tonnes as "ambitious" and "certainly not guaranteed".

"The Commission’s own data show that the EU currently has 3.54 million tonnes of CO₂ injection capacity online, while projected injection capacity is just 27.1 million tonnes, so there is clearly a significant gap to close in the remaining 4 years before the end of the decade," Rasmussen told Euronews.

He noted that the biggest hurdle ahead for carbon capture and storage in the EU is whether the technology will scale in alignment with industrial needs to deliver a viable sustainable solution — exactly what the Commission is set to propose, yet it remains unclear whether Exon's legal challenge is linked to its delay and how achievable the plan would be.

Environmental NGO Bellona warned that the lawsuit could undermine Brussels' efforts to establish a viable market for carbon capture and storage.

The group argued the case exposes how investment protections under the ECT can be used by fossil fuel companies to challenge climate legislation.

William Druet, policy advisor at Bellona Europa, said the EU rules on mandatory CO₂ injections for fossil fuel producers have an important role to play in bringing about investments.

"Meeting the EU’s climate-neutrality objectives means accelerating investments in infrastructure that will ultimately underpin a clean economy and create long-term commercial opportunities for the companies developing and operating it," Druet said.

"Investment arbitration should not become a mechanism through which companies seek compensation for being required to accelerate investments that will eventually form part of their own business models," he added, in reference to the ECT.

ExxonMobil did not respond to a Euronews request for comment.

The United Kingdom is seeking tougher penalties for damaging critical underwater infrastructure, but industry insiders warn that stronger rules alone cannot prevent widespread disruption.

As concerns over sabotage and suspicious Russian activity in European waters intensify, the United Kingdom (UK) is working on legislation that could see those deliberately damaging critical undersea infrastructure jailed for up to 14 years, according to a statement.

The proposed penalties also include unlimited fines for interfering with undersea cables and pipelines. If adopted, the changes would update legislation dating back to 1885.

The plans would introduce new security obligations for cable operators and give the government greater powers to respond to national security threats.

The government points to growing geopolitical tensions as a reason for the changes.

"The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure," said Ian Murray, Telecoms minister of the UK.

The UK's move follows a series of incidents in European waters, including the Nord Stream pipeline sabotage in 2022, damage to the Baltic connector gas pipeline in 2023 and several undersea cable failures in the Baltic Sea in 2024.

Such incidents highlight the importance of infrastructure connecting countries across Europe and beyond.

Subsea fibre-optic cables carry around 99% of intercontinental internet traffic worldwide, according to a 2025 report by the European Commission's Joint Research Centre.

Stretching thousands of kilometres across the seabed, they transmit everything from video calls and emails to financial transactions and business communications.

A severed cable does not necessarily cause an internet blackout. The global network allows data to be rerouted through alternative connections when one fails.

However, the additional traffic can overwhelm backup capacity, potentially slowing online payments, banking services and other applications that depend on reliable connectivity.

Can tougher laws make Europe's underwater networks safer?

While the UK government argues that stronger laws are necessary to deter interference and improve operators' preparedness, industry insiders warn that tougher penalties alone cannot guarantee network resilience.

"Adding more cables along the same corridors doesn't guarantee resilience," Tony O'Sullivan, CEO of international network operator RETN, which carries data across Europe, Asia and North America, told Euronews Next.

Laying new cables along existing routes is often cheaper, but they can end up sharing landing points and passing through the same narrow corridors.

"We call it 'fake diversity'," O'Sullivan said.

This means several connections could be damaged in a single incident, even when operators have invested in additional cables.

The risks extend beyond deliberate sabotage. Around 150 to 200 subsea telecommunications cable faults occur worldwide each year, with 70 to 80% caused by accidental human activity, primarily fishing and ships dragging anchors, according to a report by the International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC).

However, O'Sullivan warns that investment is not keeping pace with the growing risks.

"The fix is simple − we need more routes, subsea and on land, that go different ways. It's more expensive, but it significantly reduces the risk of a single incident taking out several routes at once and slowing down services for millions of people," he said.

How is the rest of Europe protecting its cables?

Similar efforts to strengthen underwater infrastructure are underway elsewhere in Europe.

Denmark is developing new surveillance capabilities to monitor critical underwater infrastructure, including cables and pipelines, and detect potential threats.

In February 2026, the European Commission announced a €347 million investment in strategic submarine cable projects, including €20 million to strengthen repair capabilities in the Baltic Sea.

The UK government is consulting on its proposals until 14 January 2027, with feedback expected to shape the final legislation.

Governments, doctor surgeries and even rival AI firms have been caught up, and the episode is sharpening questions about Europe's reliance on a handful of US tech giants.

A failure in part of Microsoft’s server infrastructure has cut people off from Outlook email, Teams and other everyday office tools for more than a day, with problems reported in 74 countries and territories.

The disruption began on Thursday afternoon European time and was still not fully fixed on Friday morning. Microsoft says there is no sign of a cyber attack, but it has yet to name a root cause.

Here is what we know so far.

What has happened since Thursday?

Euronews reported how the outage first hit Outlook, Teams and Copilot on Thursday evening. Since then, the picture has got worse rather than better.

Microsoft's fixes have not solved the issue. Servers it brought back overnight crashed again once traffic returned, and the company admitted its changes were "not taking as expected". By Friday morning, it reported only "marginal success".

Reports to Downdetector, a website that tracks outages using reports from the public, registered nearly 140,000 issues on Outlook alone.

The list of affected services has also grown. Microsoft's incident notice now includes SharePoint Online, used for sharing documents, and the security tool Defender XDR. The task-management apps Planner and To Do have also been reported down.

How many people have been affected?

The true number is unknown. Downdetector only counts people who file a report, so its figures are a signal of scale rather than a headcount. Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its 365 apps.

A map published by Downdetector showed users affected across the Americas and in parts of Europe, Asia and Africa. The knock-on effects reached well beyond missed emails:

Healthcare: several GP practices in the UK told patients to phone with urgent queries rather than use email or online forms.

Government: the Singaporean government and Australia's intelligence agency said they had been affected.

Tech firms: OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the tools that link their AI services to Microsoft 365.

Business: one US company, the electric vehicle maker Workhorse, postponed its earnings call to Monday.

Paul Spain, of the New Zealand-based advisory firm Gorilla Technology, said many companies had effectively "lost a business day".

What went wrong?

Microsoft has not yet named a root cause, and its explanation has shifted over the course of the outage.

It first blamed "elevated load", meaning servers were under far more strain than usual. It later clarified that this was not caused by a surge in users. Instead, a large number of servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", pushing their work onto the machines that remained.

Attention then turned to the automated "health checks" Microsoft uses to decide whether a server is fit to handle traffic. The company said it was testing a configuration change to fix a problem that was causing servers to fail those checks and drop out of service.

Mahmoud Elkhodr, a senior lecturer in information and communication technologies at CQUniversity in Australia, offered one explanation in The Conversation. Health checks are meant to pull faulty servers out of action, he wrote. If the checking system itself goes wrong, it can switch off healthy servers and overload the rest.

Elkhodr stressed that this is only an inference from Microsoft's public updates.

Was it a cyber attack, and is my data at risk?

There is no evidence of a hack. Microsoft said it was not aware of any "malicious activity", and executive vice-president Charles Lamanna said the outage did not appear to be a cyber attack. No group has claimed responsibility.

Elkhodr noted that the most common online attack used to knock services offline, known as distributed denial of service, works by flooding a system with outside traffic. That does not match up with Microsoft's statement that traffic had not increased.

That has not stopped speculation. Smitarani Tripathy, a social media analyst at the data firm GlobalData, said rumours of hacking spread on X because Microsoft offered no confirmed cause or timeline for a fix.

On the evidence so far, this is a problem of access, not of theft. An outage stops people reaching their emails and files; it does not in itself mean anyone else has seen them. Nothing Microsoft has said suggests customer data has been exposed or lost.

There are still indirect risks:

Weaker defences: Defender XDR, which organisations use to spot threats, was among the affected services, which could make security monitoring harder while it is down.

Scams: fraudsters often use major outages to send fake "support" emails or messages. Users should be wary of any message asking them to log in or reset a password, and check Microsoft's official status page instead.

Lost messages: some emails may arrive late. Users should check that anything important sent during the outage has been received.

What does it mean for Europe?

This is not a one-off. In January, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services went down for hours. In August, a faulty code update disrupted Outlook and Exchange Online for several days.

The outage also coincides with European governments and businesses debating how far they should depend on a few US cloud providers. When one of them fails, thousands of services built on top of it can fail too, including those run by other companies.

Elkhodr argued that organisations should plan for digital outages the way they prepare for natural disasters. That means having backup systems and testing them regularly, not just writing plans that are never used. For individuals, he suggested keeping essentials such as contacts available offline.

Microsoft has promised continued updates through its service status page. Until it publishes a full review, the key questions of why so many servers failed at once, and how to stop it happening again, remain unanswered.

Researchers found that dementia risk increases with the number of cigarettes smoked per day, rising by 16% for those who smoke 10 a day and by 34% for those who smoke 20, compared with people who have never smoked.

A scientific review involving about 2.8 million people found that smoking is associated with an increased risk of dementia, Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, with the risk rising as the number of cigarettes smoked per day increases.

According to the study, which was led by researchers from Curtin University in Australia and published in the journal "eClinicalMedicine", smokers face a 31% higher risk of developing dementia compared with people who have never smoked.

The risk rose to 40% for Alzheimer's disease and to 52% for vascular dementia.

The researchers observed a link between the number of cigarettes smoked per day and the likelihood of developing dementia. People who smoke 10 cigarettes a day face a 16% higher risk, while the risk rises to 34% among those who smoke 20 cigarettes a day, compared with people who have never smoked.

Lead researcher Mario Serfo said the findings show the need to pay attention to the impact of smoking on brain health, alongside its well-known risks to the heart and lungs and the likelihood of developing cancer.

He added that the relationship between smoking and dementia becomes stronger as the number of cigarettes consumed increases.

Quitting smoking may reduce the risk of developing the disease

The study showed that people who had quit smoking do not face a higher risk of developing dementia compared with those who have never smoked, and that their risk is lower than that of people who continue to smoke.

However, the researchers explained that the study's findings do not prove a direct causal relationship between smoking and dementia, although they add to the scientific evidence suggesting that quitting smoking may help reduce the risk of developing the disease.

Blossom Stephan, a co-author of the study, called for brain health to be included in discussions about the risks of smoking and the health benefits of giving it up.

The researchers stressed the need to expand tobacco control campaigns so they also warn about the impact of smoking on brain function and cognitive abilities, in addition to its well-known risks to the heart and lungs and the likelihood of developing cancer.

In this context, they recommended including warnings about brain health on cigarette packs and incorporating them into smoking cessation programmes to raise awareness of the health consequences of tobacco consumption.

The researchers called for further studies to determine whether the timing of quitting smoking and the length of abstinence affect the level of dementia risk.

A tribute band to an artist who was only known in an ultra-restricted circle while alive sent the Coliseu dos Recreios wild at its farewell concert. Understanding the José Pinhal phenomenon means grasping our century's drive to reclaim nuggets from the past.

José Pinhal is a name that, until about a decade ago or a little more, nobody knew.

Born in Santa Cruz do Bispo (Matosinhos), he had a career on the circuit of dances and nightclubs in northern Portugal in the 1980s, and died at just 41, in 1993, in a road accident as he was returning from a performance, in almost complete anonymity.

It would probably have stayed that way if our century did not have a voracious appetite for stories of nuggets rescued from the past and from oblivion, proof of that is, for example, the story of the photographer Vivian Maier, whose genius was only discovered after her death, or the plot of one of Paul Auster's biggest best-sellers, O Livro das Ilusões, in which a man trying to overcome the grief for his wife and children, killed in a plane crash, strives to rescue from oblivion an actor and director from the golden age of silent cinema (although here there is a plot twist that differs from the stories of Maier and Pinhal).

Pinhal's fate began to change on the day when the brother of Paulo Cunha Martins, a photographer and collector of musical rarities from Porto, moved into a flat that had previously housed the office of a music agent. Inside, everything had been left as it was, among the many relics the new tenant found two cassettes covered in dust.

At first they were played within a circle of friends. It was some years more before José Pinhal's songs turned into a viral phenomenon, which happened after they were uploaded to YouTube.

Songs such as "Tu És a Que Eu Quero (Tu Não Prendas o Cabelo)", later used in advertising by an online betting company, started being hummed across half of Portugal. The story reached the pages of the British newspaper The Guardian (source in Portuguese) and led to a documentary (source in Portuguese).

One mystery still had to be solved: Who was José Pinhal? The answers only started to emerge when Marina Pinhal, the singer's only daughter, commented on the video posted online in 2016, which already has around 1.4 million views.

It was also that year that José Pinhal Post-Mortem Experience appeared. The tribute band, founded to honour the singer, has now said goodbye to the stage after ten years, with a concert in the hall where Pinhal dreamed of singing one day, the Coliseu dos Recreios in Lisbon.

The band began as a joke in 2016 and was supposed to perform for only one night. In the meantime, ten years have passed. The members, all of them from the alternative music scene, have other projects they want to develop. But they wanted the finale to be total, with final concerts in the coliseums of Porto and Lisbon.

João Sarnadas is a guitarist and was the driving force behind the band, as well as being part of the collective that runs Favela Discos and having a career in experimental music under the alias "Coelho Radioactivo": "My first reaction when I heard José Pinhal's music was realising that it is something unique. Although it is something that lives within a context, the context of romantic music, of dance music, his music is something unique," he says.

In 2016 Sarnadas and some friends wanted to form a band to play Pinhal's songs, which they had been listening to obsessively, at a birthday party. Several other musicians joined them. Over the following ten years they played at dozens of parties and venues all over the country. Sarnadas says they even considered suggesting to Pinhal himself that they rescue him from oblivion and form a band that could accompany him, before they knew that he had already died.

Bruno Martins, who uses the stage name Bruno de Seda, is the singer and "wears" Pinhal's skin: "I already had the moustache," he jokes. The look is completed with Pinhal's trademark image, "more 80s would be impossible": black shirt, white suit and gold chain round his neck. "What impressed me most about him was the voice and the way he sang. That vast commitment he gave to the songs," he says.

That commitment and authenticity, which Bruno de Seda reproduces perfectly on stage, seem to be what have fascinated an entire legion of fans from various generations, largely young, urban and educated, an audience radically different from the one that usually follows this kind of music. Pinhal did not hide his strong northern accent, he sometimes sang out of tune, but always with passion and without apologising for being who he was. "We feel immense genuineness," says musician Rui Fonseca, from 800 Gondomar, in the documentary A Vida Dura Muito Pouco by Dinis Leal Machado. The music he made, together with Manuel Eduardo's arrangements, has "something", sometimes hard to explain, that sets him apart from all the others who marked Portuguese popular music or what started to be called, disparagingly, música pimba.

Yet one thing that it is very hard to ascribe to Pinhal is originality. Although most of the compositions are simply signed as "DR" (rights reserved), a visit to this playlist on Spotify (source in Portuguese) is enough to realise that José Pinhal's "greatest hits" are in fact versions of songs by Brazilian and Spanish artists of the time, such as Paco Escudero, Chiquitete or Cláudio Fontana.

For José Pinhal Post-Mortem Experience, whose final concert at the Coliseu dos Recreios will go down in history as a rare explosion of energy, it is time to declare their mission accomplished: "The message of showing who José Pinhal is and his work has been delivered. That job has been done," says Bruno de Seda. "Above all, this takes up a lot of our time. A band of this calibre requires almost total dedication and, after ten years, we already want to do other things," he concludes.

In the front row, as at most of the band's concerts, was Marina Pinhal who, besides being the singer's daughter, is also one of the tribute band's biggest fans. At this concert, because it was so special, she was emotional: "All I can do is thank the band, but it is sad that they are ending, especially in this hall, where my father so often dreamed of singing one day," she says. "I am very happy with their journey, I am very happy with my father's journey, and with everything my father does to people with his music."

The band is closing the circle, but José Pinhal's music is kept alive by all the fans he has gained since he was rediscovered, who will go on chanting the rallying cry that is always heard at the concerts: "José Pinhal, immortal!"

Swedish pop star Robyn, whose hits include 'With Every Heartbeat' and 'Dancing On My Own', shared her verdict on Eurovision during an appearance on Amy Poehler's podcast. She suggested Eurovision's appeal had diminished for her since ABBA’s involvement, and that it was "embarrassing".

Robyn is not shy about her feelings towards the Eurovision Song Contest, labelling the annual music event as "shit" and "embarrassing".

The celebrated Swedish pop star, whose hits include 'Show Me Love', 'With Every Heartbeat' and 'Dancing On My Own', shared her verdict during an appearance on comedian and actress Amy Poehler's podcast, Good Hang.

Robyn suggested Eurovision's appeal had diminished for her since ABBA’s involvement.

The Swedish pop group won Eurovision with their hit song 'Waterloo' in 1974, and since then, Sweden has won the contest six times – the latest being Loreen in 2023 with the song 'Tattoo'.

Despite this impressive track record, Robyn told Poehler that she is not a fan, admitting that she frequently finds herself cringing at what she sees.

"We don't have ABBA any more so I don't really watch Eurovision. Now it's just shit, I would say."

She added: “I have American friends I watch it with, and my friend Bert has a blanket he pulls up over his eyes when we're watching it because it's so embarrassing. It really is embarrassing."

“After I've watched it, I feel really overstimulated and in a bad way. I was looking for words – I'm not going to say – but I don't like it.”

She's not the only one, as Eurovision has taken many blows over the years, with the contest's reputation being repeatedly dented by the inclusion of Israel on the line-ups.

Last month, Dutch public broadcaster NPO reversed its earlier decision to return to the contest, after broadcaster AVROTROS had announced in August that it would not take part because of Israel's presence.

Ireland has already announced it will not take part in Eurovision 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.

The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Last year, five countries - Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland and Slovenia - boycotted Eurovision after organizers declined to exclude Israel over its military actions in Gaza and violence against Palestinians in the West Bank.

The Spanish broadcaster RTVE said at the time that it would not broadcast the contest or the semi-finals and criticised the decision-making process as “insufficient”. They said that the EBU’s decision to keep Israel as a competitor “increases RTVE’s distrust of the festival’s organisation and confirms the political pressure surrounding it."

Irish broadcaster RTÉ stated: “RTÉ feels that Ireland’s participation remains unconscionable given the appalling loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there, which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk.” As for Slovenian broadcaster RTVSLO, they said last year that taking part “would conflict with its values of peace, equality and respect” and that it was pulling out of the competition "on behalf of the 20,000 children who died in Gaza".

The 2026 competition drew 131 million viewers, down 35 million from the year before.

Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year.

As for Robyn, her latest album 'Sexistential' made the cut in Euronews Culture's Best Albums of 2026 So Far list. We wrote: "Female sexuality, motherhood and existential dread - Robyn lays it all out on the dance floor in her ninth studio album. Frothy with the Swedish singer’s trademark dopamine-laden synth-pop, ‘Sexistential’ feels like entering the eye of a hormonal storm. As she sings in the title track: “My body's a spaceship with the ovaries on hyperdrive / Got a whole universe inside that exists in between my thighs.”"

We added: "Jittery and bombastic, this collision of parental and sexual identities is overwhelmingly self-assured - the music of someone that doesn’t just write music, but owns everyone it touches. It will make you want to bury your self-doubt and give in to the fleeting elation of desire."

Raportul GLOBSEC 2026 include un sondaj făcut în 11 țări europene, între care cele de pe flancul estic, dar și Franța și Germania. Dar toți europenii cred că această armată europeană nu ar trebui să înlocuiască NATO ci să evolueze sub steagul NATO (împreună cu SUA, UK, Canada), chiar dacă sondajul arată o neliniște semnificativă legată de loialitatea americanilor față de alianță.

Astfel, deși aproximativ 77% dintre cetățenii țărilor membre NATO au declarat că ar vota ca țara lor să rămână în alianță, peste o treime dintre respondenții din țările europene chestionate consideră acum Statele Unite o amenințare la adresa securității. Aproximativ jumătate dintre respondenții din Germania, Franța și Marea Britanie au susținut această opinie, comparativ cu doar o treime din Europa Centrală și de Est.

Germanii sunt cei mai categorici (peste 50%) în a considera Washingtonul o amenințare la adresa securității, în timp ce 74% din români spun că SUA sunt un partener de securitate fiabil pentru Europa.

After Microsoft 365 services went down on 12 November, affecting millions of users worldwide, here is how you can keep using Outlook while the issue is fixed.

The disruption on Thursday 12 November mainly affected Outlook, but it also hit Teams, Copilot and the rest of the Microsoft 365 tools. According to reports collected by the Downdetector website, the outage was particularly widespread in the Americas.

Microsoft explained on X that it had received reports from users who could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes through different connection methods in the Americas, Europe, Africa and the rest of the world.

The Redmond-based company later said that part of its infrastructure was carrying a higher than normal load, which probably caused the errors, and announced that it would redistribute traffic across its systems. The Teams platform appears to be working at the moment, although some users were still reporting difficulties.

How to keep working while Outlook is not responding

The first step is to check whether the problem is still ongoing. Microsoft publishes updates on its X account, @MSFT365Status (source in Spanish), and maintains a status page at status.cloud.microsoft.

If you are an administrator, Microsoft’s documentation says that the Microsoft 365 admin centre has a service status section showing open and resolved incidents, accessible to those with the service support administrator or Helpdesk admin roles.

It is better not to expect too much from switching apps. Since the outage affects access to Exchange Online mailboxes through different connection methods, moving from the desktop app to another one may not help at all. TechRadar pointed this out during a previous outage in July 2025, when the web version, mobile app and desktop client all failed at the same time.

If you use desktop Outlook with a Microsoft 365 or Exchange account, there is a useful option. According to Microsoft, Exchange cached mode (source in Spanish) lets you work with mailbox items even when the network connection is slow or unavailable. It does not work with POP or IMAP accounts.

In addition, the Send/Receive tab includes a Work Offline button, available in Outlook for Microsoft 365 and in the 2021, 2019 and 2016 versions. It allows you to keep reading and drafting messages using the content already stored on your computer.

For the rest of your work, the suggestion is to switch to channels that do not depend on Microsoft. It proposes internal messaging tools such as Slack or Google Chat to coordinate the team, and uploading large files to WeTransfer or Google Drive so the link can be shared through another route. Teams also experienced incidents on Thursday, so it is not the safest option for this coordination, although on Friday it is working in most regions.

What alternatives to Outlook are available

If the outage leads you to consider other options, it is worth distinguishing between email providers and programs used to read your mail. Changing program does not change where your mailbox is hosted. Thunderbird, for example, can connect to a Microsoft 365 account via IMAP, but that account is still hosted on Microsoft’s servers. To rely on another provider you need to open an account with them.

Among internet providers, Arsys describes Gmail as a free service with gmail.com accounts, apps for Android and iOS and integration with Drive, Google Calendar and Google Meet. It points to two limits: storage is shared with other Google services, and to use your own domain you need Google Workspace, which is a paid service.

Kinsta lists Proton Mail, an open-source service based in Switzerland that offers end to end encryption, web access and apps for Android and iOS. It has a free plan, although custom domains are only available on paid plans.

The AI chip giant has no leader in waiting, may lose its voice in Washington, and has big bets in Europe that its founder championed in person.

For 33 years, it was almost impossible to separate Nvidia from Jensen Huang. The co-founder, always in his leather jacket, turned a company he started with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner into one of the world’s most valuable firms. He drew stadium crowds to watch him unveil the chips that power tools like ChatGPT.

His resignation on Thursday leaves the company facing a question it has never had to answer: what does Nvidia look like without him? He stepped down after admitting an affair with a woman US officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence, and after reports of a second relationship with a subordinate.

Who takes charge?

For now, chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO and keep her finance role. Harvey C. Jones, a former chief executive of chip design software firm Synopsys, becomes the board’s first-ever chair.

Kress joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years at companies including Cisco and Microsoft, and is often cited as a leading internal candidate. But the company has no known succession plan, and Huang repeatedly avoided naming an heir.

“There’s not someone who is sort of prepped and ready to go next in line,” said Carmem Domingues, who was a senior AI adviser in the Biden White House.

Martin Peers of tech outlet The Information has said there are “no obvious internal candidates”. He named two possible outside picks: AMD chief executive Lisa Su, who is a relative of Huang, and Rene Haas, CEO of British chip designer Arm. Another analyst has suggested Intel boss Lip-Bu Tan.

Huang’s children, Madison and Spencer, both hold management roles at the company. Domingues said it was unclear how ready they would be to take over.

The ‘Huang premium’

Investors have long paid extra for Nvidia’s leadership.

"Investors have effectively been buying into Nvidia’s technology and Huang’s vision in equal measure," said Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management. "It may now have to calculate how much of that premium was attached to one individual."

Mandeep Singh, global head of technology research at Bloomberg Intelligence, said Nvidia was unlikely to be “as aggressive” under new leadership. That matters for a company racing to deliver each new generation of AI chips.

Rivals could gain as customers look to spread their orders. Charu Chanana of Saxo Markets said “AI leadership could broaden, rather than the boom ending”, and named AMD, Broadcom, Alphabet and Samsung as possible winners.

The first test comes on 17 November, when Nvidia reports its quarterly results under interim leadership.

Ripples across the AI industry

The bigger fear is contagion. Nvidia sits at the base of an AI economy in which companies fund one another in a loop.

"All the AI companies either owe money to Nvidia and/or depend on them," said Domingues. "One falling can bring down a lot."

Chanana said the "bigger risk is a disruption to AI spending itself". Financing, cloud giants’ spending and the returns on AI investment were already under scrutiny. The turmoil also comes days before AI firm Anthropic’s stock market debut, which is widely seen as a test of investor appetite for the sector.

Not everyone is alarmed. Investor Sheikha Maytha Bint Maktoum said any disruption would be "temporary", given the ecosystem Nvidia has built over decades.

What it means for Europe

Europe has a lot riding on what Nvidia does next. A few weeks ago, at an investment summit in Berlin, Germany, Huang agreed an AI partnership with Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The federal government is reportedly contributing a nine-figure sum in euros.

Around a dozen German companies are expected to take part, including Siemens, Audi and start-up Black Forest Labs, which is based in Freiburg im Breisgau.

Nvidia says it invested almost $1 billion (€900 million) in Germany in 2025. In October, it announced an AI hub for start-ups in Stockholm, Sweden.

Huang championed those projects personally. It remains to be seen whether his successor shares his enthusiasm for each country building a “national intelligence” from its own data.

Losing its voice in Washington

Huang was a close informal adviser on AI to US President Donald Trump, and spent years lobbying against curbs on sales of advanced chips to China. Last year, Trump cleared Nvidia’s H200 chips for export there, overruling China hawks in both parties.

With Huang gone and the spy allegations hanging over the company, that influence may fade. Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have already asked the administration to preserve all documents on Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Beijing denies the spying claims and has accused Washington of using them as a pretext for a technological “blockade”. Meanwhile, Chinese firms are trying to break their dependence on US suppliers, and Huawei is presenting itself as China’s answer to Nvidia.

Equity markets mostly fell on Friday, following losses on Wall Street as investors weighed what Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia could mean for the AI industry. Oil prices rose after US President Donald Trump said Washington did not need a deal with Iran.

European and Asian shares mostly fell on Friday as investors weighed what Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO could mean for the global artificial intelligence industry.

European stock indices opened lower, with the FTSE 100 in London down 0.2% at the open, and the benchmark indices down 0.3% in Paris and Frankfurt. US stock futures also edged lower, including the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100.

In the US, Nvidia shares had closed down 4.3% on Thursday. The S&P 500, the Nasdaq Composite and the Dow Jones Industrial Average each fell about 0.4%, with the Dow closing at 52,297.09. Some Nvidia rivals gained, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), which rose 5.9%.

Nvidia said on Thursday that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect. The announcement followed reports of two affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China, which raised US national security concerns. Nvidia’s long-serving chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in as interim CEO.

The departure of Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and was a key architect of its AI strategy and the broader global AI boom, has raised questions about how it could affect the development of the technology. Huang had been the face of Nvidia and was seen by some in the industry as bigger than the company itself.

Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said he does not expect any short-term impact on the company, provided its order book remains strong and it continues to deliver on its performance targets.

Barringer added: “What this news threatens to do is harm the wider AI ecosystem in the longer term. Huang is hugely influential in the debates around AI regulation and has developed Nvidia into the leader in AI investment and financing. With his voice now removed from the table, and the potential for Nvidia to pivot on its strategy over time, the company may not carry the sway it once did.”

Many AI hardware stocks across Asia have been highly dependent on the pace of AI infrastructure development in the US.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 closed up 0.5% at 61,142.35, while South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.0% to close at 5,290.53. Shanghai’s Composite closed 0.6% lower at 3,634.35, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was down more than 1.5% at 23,637.60 at around 09:00 GMT.

Chip stocks were mixed on Friday. At the 07:30 CET close in Tokyo, Tokyo Electron rose 1.7%, while Kioxia fell 2.2% and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 5.1%. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics fell 1.0%, and SK Hynix dropped 3.2%.

Taiwan’s Taiex closed 1.35% higher at 43,675.12, with TSMC up 0.43%, and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 closed down 0.7% at 9,082.20.

Stocks were also under broad pressure from an increase in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US didn't “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he posted on social media. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

At around 07:00 GMT, Brent crude was up 0.7% at $96.48 a barrel, compared with roughly $72 a barrel before the Iran war began in late February. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate rose 0.2% to $88.91 a barrel.

US gold futures for December delivery edged up to $3,899.00 a troy ounce in European morning trade.

In currency markets, the euro rose to $1.1061 from $1.1055 on Thursday and strengthened to 83.60 pence from 83.53 pence. Sterling fell to $1.3229 from $1.3235, while the dollar eased to 159.79 yen from 159.84 yen.

Thousands of young Catholics gathered at Peru's National Stadium in Lima on Thursday 12 November for a prayer vigil led by Pope Leo XIV, transforming the venue into a sea of lights, The stands lit up with thousands of mobile phone lights as the pontiff led an evening of songs, prayer and reflection.

A sea of swaying lights, a jubilant nun and worshippers holding candles filled the scene as the pontiff addressed the crowd at Lima's National Stadium. Arriving in an open-sided vehicle, the 71-year-old pope smiled and waved to cheering spectators, some of whom ran alongside his escort while others held up placards, balloons and miniature figures of him. As darkness fell, tens of thousands switched on their phone torches, illuminating the stands amid a chorus of singing and chanting.

The evening gathering brought together young Peruvian Catholics and students for a moment of prayer and reflection during the final leg of Pope Leo XIV's 12-day tour of South America, following visits to Uruguay and Argentina. Around 60,000 people packed the stadium, with an estimated 300,000 more gathered outside.

For the American-born pope, the visit carries deep personal significance. He spent more than two decades serving the Church in Peru, including as Bishop of Chiclayo, and became a naturalised Peruvian citizen in 2015 under his birth name, Robert Prevost. Having long described the country as his "homeland", he has been welcomed back by jubilant crowds who still affectionately remember him as "Padre Roberto", particularly at the lively youth vigil.

New York in the 1960s, like much of the United States, is unrecognisable from the land many of us know today. French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont captured all manner of daily life in the city, and beyond, in a stunning new book, "Rebels with a Cause".

Dirty, dangerous and turbulent. When French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont landed in New York in the 1960s his plan was to record ordinary lives from an outsider's perspective.

From civil and gay rights to anti-Vietnam war protests, he soon discovered a city on the edge of a cultural revolution, driven by movements, rebelling against the firmly fixed and established norms.

Much has been written recently about the deep splits which divide the United States, and Laffont's work perfectly illustrates some of the roots of the "revolutions that continue to shape" the entire country today.

In a wide ranging conversation with European Lens, Laffont reflects on his time spent documenting America and shares his views on the future of photography.

Jean-Pierre Laffont: Well, I arrived in the United States in April 1964, at a time when... Actually, I didn't arrive in the United States first, I arrived in New York, in New York City, and besides, I didn't have any money to go anywhere else. And I found myself in a city where everything was in ruins, where everything was dirty, where crime was everywhere.

I lived on the West Side, and it was dangerous to walk around at night. It was a city where I realised that if I walked around with my cameras hanging around my neck, I was putting myself at risk. It was a city on the verge of bankruptcy.

Anything new is a source of visual excitement, for a photographer. You see things, you notice them, you frame them, you compose the shot. Basically, they're easy to see and photograph.

I actually realised that the young people out on the streets weren't necessarily against the Vietnam War, which wasn't their war, and which they didn't understand. What it was really about was the injustice of the way they were being drafted. At the time, the American draft was a lottery.

Some could stay in school and continue their university studies, while others, on the contrary, were forced to leave because, unfortunately, they had drawn the short straw. They were the ones who had to go.

On top of that, two or three years later, around 1971 or 1972, there were many young Black Americans being sent off, and they really were being sent into the meat grinder; they were actually assigned to combat units. And that, too, was an injustice that was beginning to become apparent.

All these movements that began in New York often ended in Washington, where I went as well. These were movements that started spontaneously.

Gay Pride

One of the first that I remember experiencing very clearly was joyful. It was a joyful rebellion. It was the first Gay Pride, in June 1970. They arrived in Central Park and started kissing, they started dancing, and for me, it was a fantastic day.

I didn't know it was the first Gay Pride. It was an extraordinary gay celebration, a beautiful event, full of joy, among both women and men. And it was absolutely extraordinary to photograph.

I went back ten years later for the tenth Gay Pride, but this time I went to cover the major gay movement in San Francisco.

There was a mayor, there were doctors, there were mechanics, there were restaurants, there were lawyers, there were gay architects, serving gay people and wanting to work only with gay people.

It was a very interesting, very intelligent community, but ultimately, they were rebels. It wasn't a revolution; it was a rebellion.

It was against the system as it stood, and San Francisco did it extraordinarily well.

Past and present perfect

I used to have five cameras around me when I went out to certain areas, because I had long lenses, and there was no time to change them.

Today's young photographers are incredibly lucky - they don't have to reload their cameras, they don't have to think, "That's it, I've got 36 shots left", they don't have to worry about their flash, because cameras can take pictures even at night, without a flash, nowadays.

A photograph always says more than a film, more than television.<br><br>

Now everything is done automatically. On top of that, the camera tells you where you took the picture, when you took it, so you no longer lose it.

I've lost hundreds of thousands of photographs that were handed over to my clients, because that's how agencies worked. The first photographs went to the best magazine, and then we gave them the originals, which I never saw again, which I never got back, which were lost, and which may now be in the archives of some major magazines, but in any case, they're no longer in my archives.

Altered reality

I'm not yet sufficiently familiar with artificial intelligence. Many people see it as a huge threat because of bad photos, altered photos, and manipulated images.

I come from a generation when altering your negative was simply out of the question. I was a witness to my times, and I never manipulated a photograph.

You should understand immediately what is happening [in a photojournalistic photograph]. It's an accident, it's a happy moment, it's a demonstration against something.

We need these photographs. A photograph always says more than a film, more than television. We remember a still image more than a moving image, every time. And we need that. There will always be a need for witnesses.

"Rebels with a Cause", published by Damiani Books, is available now.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Ireland this week following a visit to the Kremlin, after which they pushed for Europeans to be present at the negotiating table in future talks.

The pair landed at a military base near Dublin on Thursday, where they addressed the media alongside Zelenskyy.

Other matters, such as a ceasefire - or any concrete steps towards ending the war - took a back seat as the key point of progress announced by the trio was that European negotiators would be involved in future discussions on ending Russia's all-out war on Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told reporters that Europe would have a "voice" during future talks and that it would not be kept "separately" on the sidelines - as had happened in recent trilateral negotiations between US, Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi.

"This is important for us because the war is in Europe. We will be member of EU in the future and that's why it's very important. For prosperity and for security guarantees it's very important to have Europe," Zelenskyy said.

In a post on X, Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, added: "Both sides have now agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include our European partners."

"This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia," he wrote.

Moscow has not confirmed whether it has agreed to include European negotiators in subsequent talks.

In comments shared by the Russian foreign ministry on Friday morning, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said: "For our part, the position of the Europeans has been comprehensively outlined. They are striving by every means possible to join the negotiations, but, as our President has said, they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war."

It comes after Witkoff and Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier this week.

During their meeting, Putin signalled that Russia would not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country, dampening hopes of a nearing deal to end the war.

Some people are turning to rented options as a green alternative to fresh-cut or artificial Christmas trees.

With December on the horizon, an annual debate is brewing: should I get a real or fake Christmas tree?

Artificial Christmas tree lovers may have already resurrected their old family favourite, bringing the dusty box out of the attic as the festive season begins. Those who opt for fresh cut might be yet to make their pilgrimage to a local Christmas tree farm, convinced the nostalgic smell of pine and sense of tradition is well worth the yearly fuss.

Whether you are wrestling with a tangled wire mess or trying to tie a too-big fir to the roof of your car, you might be wondering, is a fake or real Christmas tree more sustainable?

As with most environmentally responsible choices, it's not a straightforward answer. Which one you should go for depends on a number of factors, from where you buy your tree to how you get rid of it come January.

What's the most sustainable Christmas tree option?

There is a lot of conflicting information out there about what type of Christmas tree is the most sustainable.

It is often claimed that an artificial tree is actually greener as the CO2 emitted by its production is spread across the years you use it. This can be true but it requires a long term commitment. The Carbon Trust says that a plastic pine has to be used for seven to 20 years for it to have a lower footprint than a real one.

That’s a long time when you consider that 14 per cent of artificial tree buyers in the UK plan to throw theirs away after just one use, according to research carried out in 2017.

“If you’ve got a fake tree already, keep using it – make it last as long as possible,” says Friends of the Earth tree campaigner, Emi Murphy, “but look into more environmentally-sound options when it eventually comes to replacing it.”

When looking for an artificial tree, Friends of the Earth recommends you try to find one secondhand from charity shops or online selling sites instead of buying new.

How to choose a sustainable fresh-cut Christmas tree

If you aren’t ready to make that kind of devotion to a plastic pine, then a real, fresh-cut tree might be a better option for you.

Make sure that you look for FSC-certified trees as an assurance that it has been grown sustainably in an environmentally responsible way. It’s also important to seek out places selling locally grown trees as a vast number are sent all over Europe from commercial tree producers in Denmark and Germany.

Woodland charity Grown in Britain found that €3.3 million worth of imported trees were being sold to unaware Britons in 2017 – this is often the case across the continent too. It is worth having a look at what is available close to you, as some companies will even deliver from small sustainable farms straight to your door.

How to rent a Christmas tree

Both of these traditional options, however, might soon be a thing of the past. A shift in attitude in recent years has triggered real innovation as businesses attempt to appeal to the responsible consumer. Christmas shopping doesn’t seem to have escaped that conscious shift and novel solutions, like renting a potted tree, have started to receive a lot of attention.

One company, London Christmas Tree Rental, regularly sells out of stock well in advance of the festive season.

"It just felt so wasteful for these beautiful trees to grow just for the sake of three weeks of our pleasure," Catherine Loveless, co-founder of the company, tells Euronews Earth.

It was this thought that led her and co-founder Jonathan Mearns to discover the damage done by real trees when they end up in landfill.

To reduce waste and environmental impact, the company offers a living tree, delivered straight to your front door at the beginning of December. Provided in a pot, it can be decorated, put it in pride of place and even named. Once January rolls around, they will contact you to arrange a collection so that the tree can be taken back to the farm and looked after to live another year. If you do name your tree, there is even a chance that next year you can get the same one back.

"It will have grown, changed shape slightly over the year and we love the idea of being excited to welcome it into your home like a long lost friend," says Loveless.

How to get rid of your Christmas tree

Once the big day has passed, getting rid of your tree in an eco-friendly way can cause more environmental concern. As many of us who have walked through the January Christmas tree graveyard can attest, a lot of real trees end up dumped unceremoniously on roadsides or pavements. Assuming that you’ve already ditched the plastic decorations, it will just degrade naturally, right?

Despite being wholly plant material, cut real trees still need to be properly recycled. An average two-metre-tall tree left to decompose in landfill releases around 16kg of CO2 whilst also producing methane, a gas that has up to 30 times more global warming potential than CO2 over a 100-year timespan.

The Carbon Trust says that burning or chipping your tree can reduce this carbon footprint by up to 80 per cent down to just 3.5kg of CO2.

Instead of abandoning your pine on the pavement, check if your local authority offers a tree collection scheme, which will see your wilted Christmas decoration chipped and used to cover pathways or composted to feed plants in public spaces.

Artificial trees cannot be recycled but that doesn’t mean that their life has to end when you don’t want them anymore. Voluntary organisations, churches and charities may well accept them if they are in good condition.

This generally counts as a negative against the artificial tree though, as if it makes its way to landfill it could contribute to the planet’s ongoing plastic pollution problem. Ocean Conservancy even found an artificial tree washed up on a beach during their 2018 International Coastal Cleanup.

A version of this article was first published in 2019.

The Australian actress will be celebrated at next year's Césars with France's highest film honour.

Celebrated Australian actress Nicole Kidman is set to receive an honorary César Award – France's highest film honour and the French equivalent to the Oscar.

The Académie des Arts et Techniques du Cinéma, the French film academy behind the awards, announced the honour alongside broadcaster Canal+, saying the award recognises a perfromer and producer who has never allowed fame to steer the work she chooses.

Kidman will receive the award at the 52nd ceremony on 25 February 2027 at the Olympia in Paris.

Kidman gained international fame in 1989 with her role in Dead Calm and went on to star in films like Days Of Thunder, Practical Magic, Eyes Wide Shut, Moulin Rouge!, The Others and Dogville.

She won the Oscar for Best Actress in 2003 for playing Virginia Woolf in The Hours, and in 2024 won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress at the Venice Film Festival for Babygirl.

Kidman also co-founded Blossom Films, the company behind series including Big Little Lies, The Undoing and Nine Perfect Strangers, all of which she also headlined. She won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited Series or Movie for Big Little Lies.

Previous honours include being named a Companion of the Order of Australia in 2006, receiving Cannes Film Festival’s 70th anniversary prize in 2017, and being feted by the American Film Institute in 2024 with the Lifetime Achievement Award - making her the first Australian to receive it.

Away from the screen, Kidman has served as a goodwill ambassador for UNICEF since 1994 and UN Women goodwill ambassador since 2006. She has helped raise several million dollars for women’s cancer programs, including at Stanford and the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center.

The 52nd ceremony of the Césars takes place on 25 February 2027.

Good morning. I’m Luca Bertuzzi, holding the pen for today’s newsletter. The Ukraine peace talks, and the question of who should speak for Europe at the table, have swamped the informal EU summit, kicking off another round of the name game.

Ukraine talks take over. Today was meant to be the first European Council summit dedicated to artificial intelligence. President António Costa had invited Arthur Mensch, CEO of Europe’s AI darling Mistral, and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton to discuss the opportunities and risks of the disruptive technology.

As an EU official put it, “sometimes [the European Council] gets overcrowded by current events.” And that is precisely the case, with the peace talks on Ukraine firmly at centre stage.

Late last night, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at a military airbase outside Dublin, Shona Murray reports from the ground.

The short meeting was hastily arranged in the aftermath of two days of talks in Abu Dhabi. Witkoff and Kushner arrived at the air corps barracks in cold, bleak conditions, straight from a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

A place at the table. Zelenskyy confirmed that Europe will take part directly in the next round of negotiations, rather than being kept on the sidelines. Witkoff had already floated that Putin had agreed to open the negotiating table to the Europeans, though the Kremlin quickly played down the prospect.

“Next time, next meeting, Europe ... will be in the negotiating team,” he told journalists waiting outside. Kushner also made clear that Europe’s involvement was now a given, saying a deal to end the war in Ukraine couldn’t emerge without European countries at the table.

“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table. We’ve been telling President Putin that we believe that’s very important, and President Zelenskyy has been a very strong supporter, and he’s been saying that from the very, very beginning.

“And I think that we’re able to achieve that with President Putin, and he is willing to give it a try,” Kushner said.

As Zelenskyy made his way towards his aircraft, Shona managed to ask him what the US envoys had told him about Putin’s demands following their meeting in Moscow. He declined to go into detail, saying only that everything would “depend on when and how the war will end in Ukraine”.

Europe’s security architecture. Earlier yesterday, Zelenskyy warned Europe to pay close attention to the ongoing cooperation between Washington and Moscow, and to what it could mean for the continent’s security architecture.

“It’s more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia,” Zelenskyy told the European Political Community summit in Dublin. “We are waiting for more details, and Europe needs to pay close attention,” he added.

Russia has indeed tried to turn the negotiations into a broader restructuring of Europe’s security architecture. EU leaders have rebuffed the move as an attempt to divert attention from Moscow’s battlefield setbacks and re-establish its sphere of influence.

At the EPC meeting yesterday, 43 countries signed a declaration on the key principles for the future of European security, stressing that any matter on European security must be decided by Europeans.

The signatories also “underline the necessity to provide robust and credible security guarantees to Ukraine and reiterate, for those concerned, their intention to do so, in order to prevent the recurrence of aggression in Europe in the future.”

EU peace envoy. To make sure the EU has a voice when the future of Ukraine and European security are decided, the bloc’s leaders can no longer dodge the question of who will represent them at the table, especially now that a seat may actually be on offer.

Italian PM Giorgia Meloni was the first to raise the issue again, warning that the different formats risked undermining Europe’s credibility and calling for someone with a clear mandate to join the talks. Rome has since secured a place for Meloni’s sherpa, Fabrizio Saggio, alongside his E3 counterparts in Abu Dhabi.

Speaking to reporters ahead of the summit, Meloni said Italy’s presence in the negotiations does not change her call to streamline the approach. “We need to identify who should represent European interests and with which mandate,” she said. “When we talk about the security of European nations, we are talking about making commitments about countries not present at the table.”

By contrast, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, whose country is the other major player excluded from the E3 format, tried to lower the temperature. “I do not feel that Poland is suffering from a lack of participation. Quite the opposite. As I have told you many times, I sometimes feel there are too many meetings,” he said.

The name game. Who is it going to be, then? For Luxembourg’s Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Costa is the natural choice. “We, as heads of government, have a representative. And that is President Costa,” he told the press on Thursday.

Costa has earned the trust of many leaders by cautiously building a reputation as an honest, even-handed broker. His most notable misstep came in June, when his head of cabinet, Pedro Lourtie, tried to open a diplomatic channel with Moscow.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has also pitched herself, alongside Costa, to represent the bloc in the negotiations, pointing out that the decision on who should deal with Russia was taken when she was offered the post in 2024. However, some EU leaders see Kallas as an anti-Russian hardliner, which may not help her case for a mandate.

If no final decision on the peace envoy is taken today, it will be postponed to the special summit at the end of the month, which is already loaded with the deadly combination of the EU budget and financing for Ukraine.

Kyiv is shieldless (again). Ukraine’s air defences face mounting strain as renewed restrictions on Starshield satellite services compound a chronic shortage of anti-ballistic interceptors.

Zelenskyy confirmed on Thursday that restrictions had been reintroduced on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, hampering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones. Similar restrictions had been lifted less than three weeks earlier.

Following his meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Dublin, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 115 missiles of various types in the first week of November alone, alongside thousands of guided aerial bombs and jet-powered drones.

He warned that Moscow is exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of anti-ballistic interceptors to target its energy infrastructure, urging allies to ensure Kyiv is not left with empty air defence launchers as peace negotiations continue. “Artificial restrictions do not serve peace – they serve the aggressor,” Zelenskyy said.

End of the year rush. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said her executive will present an option paper on how to cover Ukraine’s financial needs in 2027, along with the 22nd sanctions package, at the special European Council on 26-27 November.

The timing for the sanctions package is particularly tight. The secretive bilateral meetings with EU governments, dubbed “confessionals” in ecclesiastical fashion, have yet to start because Costa has been busy consulting member states on the EU budget.

The aim is to adopt the package by the end of the year, so that Putin and the Russian elite have a nice Christmas present to unpack. But some EU countries are already grumbling that, if Europe is serious about the peace talks, another round of sanctions might send the wrong message.

Barbs with Beijing. China is set to top the agenda of Brussels’ two-day Foreign Affairs Council early next week. Angela Skujins has learned from EU insiders that Kallas intends to take aim at Beijing for supplying dual-use technology to the Kremlin and allegedly training Russian soldiers.

Sanctions remain the EU’s main instrument to deter Chinese companies and entities from propping up Moscow on the battlefield. But Kallas’ approach is drawing criticism from member states, who say she overrelies on sanctions in her diplomacy, which also risks triggering a cascading tit-for-tat dispute.

FAC (Ukraine). Foreign and defence ministers from the 27 EU member states will also hear directly from Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara on the situation on the frontline, as well as energy resilience and air defence.

US Undersecretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby will also join Tuesday’s defence ministerial to discuss the transatlantic alliance. Expect no surprises on that item, with EU officials anticipating an update on the Pentagon’s ongoing force posture review.

Notable absences. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever are due to miss today’s summit because of domestic turbulence. Both have given a mandate to Luxembourg’s Frieden, who will represent the whole of Benelux.

Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who faces a snap election on 29 November, will also skip the summit. That means both governments that have put forward candidates to head the European Central Bank will be absent today.

But the Spanish candidate, Pablo Hernández de Cos, seems to have received France's support as part of a broader agreement with Germany, the FT reported.

Preparing is caring. The EU is stepping up preparations to help Ukraine survive another winter of freezing temperatures and devastating attacks on civilian energy infrastructure.

The bloc is mobilising 500 generators from its rescEU reserves, helping set up emergency support centres and supplying essential equipment, according to a joint statement from Costa and von der Leyen. Norway is expected to provide 200 buses and four floating bridges.

What needs to be done. The IMF's Europe Director Mateusz Szczurek told Europe Today EU governments need to follow a very simple economic recipe that could also help reduce political instability.

"What needs to be done is to stabilise public debt, and make sure that growth accelerates. These growth-enhancing reforms will also reduce the political tensions within countries: when wages grow, when prosperity grows, then the political pressure also falls," he said.

House prices outpaced household incomes in 17 EU countries between 2015 and 2025. The gap widened most in Portugal, while Romania saw the biggest fall in house prices relative to incomes.

How far does a household’s income go when buying a home? In 17 EU countries, it bought less in 2025 than it did a decade earlier. Eurostat’s house price-to-income ratio, showing how household income is changing relative to house prices, rose by 6.8% across the EU over that period, though it fell in 10 member states.

Meanwhile, house prices in the EU rose by 62% in the ten years to the second quarter of 2026. In response to the housing crisis across the bloc, the European Commission presented its European Affordable Housing Plan in December 2025.

What is the house price-to-income ratio?

The house price-to-income ratio compares changes in house prices with changes in disposable household income per person. A rise means homes have become more expensive relative to incomes. A fall means they have become cheaper relative to incomes.

Each country’s figure shows how far its own ratio has moved over time. Mortgage costs also affect how much buyers can afford.

Portugal records the biggest rise

Between 2015 and 2025, Portugal recorded the largest increase in the house price-to-income ratio, at 60.8%. The Netherlands followed at 34.3%.

“The country experienced a touristic boom, and their golden visa program attracted foreign investors, so house prices grew partly because of foreign capital,” Mike Langen, senior housing economist at ABN AMRO, told Euronews Business.

He said a housing shortage and demand from investors were the main reasons for the rise in the Netherlands.

The ratio also jumped by more than 20% in Hungary (26.5%), Czechia (25.8%), Spain (24.5%) and Greece (22.5%).

This means homes became less affordable in these countries, as house prices rose faster than incomes.

Ronan Lyons, an associate professor of economics at Trinity College Dublin, said the countries at the top of the list combine strong demand in their main cities with supply that has struggled to keep up.

The ratio also rose by more than 10% in Slovenia (18.2%), Ireland (14.4%), Austria (13.6%), Slovakia (11.2%), Luxembourg (10.6%) and Lithuania (10.1%).

Romania records the biggest fall as renters face high costs

At the other end, Romania’s ratio fell by 42.8%, the biggest drop in the EU. House prices were substantially lower relative to household incomes in 2025 than in 2015.

The house price-to-income ratio also fell by 25.2% in Finland and 16.2% in Bulgaria. Cyprus (12%) and Italy (11.9%) also recorded double-digit declines.

Langen said strong income growth in Bulgaria and Romania after they joined the EU made homes cheaper relative to incomes.

Lyons pointed to the pressure on renters in Romania. In 2025, 56% of people paying market rent lived in households that spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing, the highest share in the EU.

Among the EU’s four largest economies, the ratio fell by less than 6% in France and by 11.9% in Italy, while it rose by 1.6% in Germany. Spain recorded the largest increase among the four, at 24.5%.

Long-term comparison

Eurostat also compares each country’s 2025 ratio with its own average over the period from 2000 to 2025, using the earliest available year where data for 2000 are missing. Across the EU, the ratio was just 0.03% above its long-term average.

Portugal and Romania were again at opposite ends of the range. Portugal’s ratio was 37% above its long-term average, compared with a 60.8% rise from 2015. Romania’s ratio was 53% below its long-term average, compared with a 42.8% fall from 2015.

The two measures tell different stories in some countries. For example, Ireland’s ratio was 14.4% higher than in 2015 but 1.7% below its long-term average. According to Lyons, this is partly because the long-term average includes the housing bubble of the mid-2000s.

Lithuania shows a similar pattern, with a ratio 10.1% higher than in 2015 and 5.7% below its long-term average.

The Netherlands and Hungary both recorded double-digit rises between 2015 and 2025. In 2025, their ratios were 12% and 5.3% above their long-term averages, respectively. Bulgaria’s ratio was 36% below its long-term average and 16.2% below its 2015 level.

Does the starting year matter?

“The reference period (2015) showed a nearly historic low in price-to-income ratios. This means we are comparing to one of the cheapest periods in the last 20 years,” Langen said. With 2005 as the starting point, the increase would be much smaller, he added.

Langen also noted that mortgage costs matter, as few people buy homes in cash. The European Central Bank’s deposit rate is 2.5%, compared with minus 0.3% at the end of 2015.

“Both measures are about change: change since 2015, or distance from a 25-year average. Neither tells us how affordable housing is today,” Lyons said. He underlined that a fall does not make a market affordable.

Lyons drew attention to another point. “The countries ‘improving’ in the Eurostat figures do not always look good,” he said. He noted that tenants in Finland, where the ratio fell by a quarter, spend about 32% of their income on rent, the highest in the EU, according to Eurostat’s survey on income and living conditions.
