Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO, the risk of an AI bubble and soaring US debt were in focus on a packed last day of the Web Summit in Lisbon, as speakers on a panel moderated by Euronews warned that public debt markets could trigger the next financial crisis.

Jensen Huang's sudden exit as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, the risk of an AI bubble and mounting US debt took the main stage on Thursday, a packed final day of the Web Summit in Lisbon, one of Europe's largest tech conferences.

Speakers on a panel moderated by Euronews warned that public debt markets could set off the next financial crisis.

The panel featured Adam Kobeissi, founder and editor-in-chief of The Kobeissi Letter, a capital markets publication with millions of followers, and economist James Galbraith, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

It was one of many sessions squeezed into Thursday after Wednesday's programme was called off on the advice of the Portuguese government, which had declared a state of emergency ahead of Storm Charles.

Ultimately, the storm did not hit Lisbon, which only saw heavy rain and minor flooding.

Huang's exit is "a net negative for investors"

Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of two extramarital affairs.

US intelligence reportedly suspects one of the women was spying for China, claims Beijing rejects. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor.

Nvidia stock dropped roughly 15% at the open on Thursday but has since pared losses and is down a little over 5% on the day to around $164 per share, at the time of writing.

Since the all-time high price of $243 per share it hit on Monday 5 October, it is down over 30%.

Kobeissi said Huang should not have resigned and that his departure "will be a net negative for investors" over the next couple of years, though he remained bullish on Nvidia overall.

He also did not expect Huang's exit to affect next week's stock market debut of Anthropic, the AI firm behind the Claude models, which is seeking a valuation of as much as $1.4 trillion (€1.25tn).

Nvidia is among seven tech companies that have agreed to buy Anthropic shares at the offer price.

AI, China, US debt and midterm elections

Professor Galbraith said there was a good possibility that Chinese technology would eventually undercut Nvidia's, which would raise questions about the hundreds of billions that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and other hyperscalers are currently pouring into AI infrastructure.

He framed the global economy as a contest between two systems.

The US makes it easy to raise private money quickly but is slower to set policy and take decisions, he explained, while China can centralise research, technological development and deployment, and intervene more directly in its economy.

For those reasons, Galbraith said he "would tentatively bet on China" to win the AI race, and perhaps to become the world's largest economy over the next few decades.

Beyond the AI boom, the panel pointed to public debt markets as a major concern.

Kobeissi warned that one in five dollars spent by the US government goes towards paying interest on the debt, "not even to pay down the debt". US Treasury data shows Washington spent $1.1 trillion (€988bn) on net interest in the fiscal year to September, or 19% of its revenue.

"US debt to GDP ratio is at World War II levels and there has not been a technical recession since the COVID-19 pandemic," Kobeissi said, adding that "the debt market has been screaming that it will be in a higher for longer environment in the foreseeable future," meaning interest rates are set to stay high.

"On the current path the US is on, there is a 100% chance of bankruptcy," he warned, adding that central banks cannot bring down interest rates in the current environment.

Still, "we are not in an imminent 2008 situation but the trends 10 or 20 years out are very concerning," Kobeissi said, although he remains "a huge bull" on the US, citing its resilient economy and accelerating innovation.

Professor Galbraith recalled how, during the COVID-19 pandemic, US President Donald Trump and a Democratic-controlled House agreed on relief to rescue the markets, but warned that the same cohesion might be lacking now.

In last week's US midterm elections, Democrats won 255 House seats to the Republicans' 169, according to AP's count as of the time of writing. Several US states are still tabulating ballots and Democrats can still flip the Alaska Senate seat and multiple of the 16 uncalled House seats.

When asked to make a prediction, Professor Galbraith stated that "the nature of financial crises is that we cannot foresee them," though he saw concerning signs.

“Solar is the fuel, the battery is the power plant. The whole system only becomes cheaper if these work in harmony with one another.”

Europe could save 40 per cent on electricity costs thanks to solar and batteries – but only if the complimentary technologies are deployed correctly.

Solar has rapidly become a leader in clean energy, helping the world transition away from polluting fossil fuels and cushioning households from volatile oil and gas price spikes.

According to the Solar Power Europe association, harnessing sunlight for energy has saved the EU €43.7 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the 2026 US-led war on Iran.

But solar’s rapid expansion has shone a light on the urgent need for battery energy storage systems, to help prevent clean energy from being wasted when generation outstrips demand.

A new report launched during the UN COP31 climate summit has revealed just how much this combination can shape total electricity costs in Europe.

Will Europe’s solar and battery boom pay off?

The report, from the Schneider Electric Research Institute (SERI), modelled 40,500 scenarios across different combinations of solar, battery and grid costs to identify whether the rise of distributed energy resources (DERs) will ultimately raise or lower electricity costs overall.

DERs are small-scale, decentralised energy technologies like rooftop solar, battery storage systems, EVs and smart appliances.

It found that, when DER deployment is coordinated with electrification, the overall cost of running the electricity system could be cut by as much as 40 per cent by the 2030s as these technologies scale up.

These savings could translate into an additional 0.8 per cent of GDP to the global economy by 2030.

Electrification (replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives) has become a flashpoint discussion at COP31, following Türkiye’s 35-by-35 pledge.

The co-host nation wants to raise the global share of energy demand met by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 23 per cent today, by 2035 – as announced back in June.

A new study published yesterday (12 November), found that an electrified world would waste 61 per cent less energy while delivering the same services. This is partly because much of the energy produced by burning fossil fuels escapes as waste heat, making it far less efficient.

But critics say, unless sourcing electricity from clean power is specified in the final text, the pledge could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets – a move they warn would “seriously undermine climate goals”.

Europe urged to ‘accelerate’ electrification

But adding more batteries to Europe’s grid could help the continent electrify by taking advantage of surplus solar power.

In fact, the report found that battery deployment was one of the most significant variables affecting total system costs by reducing pressure during peak periods.

Get the balance wrong, and SERI warns that a mismatch of battery durations across asset types can push total system costs to as much as 35 per cent above the current benchmark.

As Laurent Bataille, SERI's EVP of Europe Operations, says: “Solar is the fuel, the battery is the power plant.

“Ultimately, batteries are making solar much more interesting. But the whole system only becomes cheaper if these work in harmony with one another. That also means building the electricity demand to use them, not just focusing on adding supply.”

Bataille argues that the priority now must be “accelerating electrified demand” and enabling more flexible energy use to “flatten the load curve and free up capacity”.

EU leaders meet in Dublin on Friday for their first AI discussion, with Mistral’s Arthur Mensch and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton as guests. But the row over who should speak for Europe in Ukraine peace talks is set to dominate.

EU leaders gather in Dublin on Friday to discuss artificial intelligence for the first time, but tensions over who should represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks are set to dominate the agenda.

European Council President António Costa has put AI on the leaders’ agenda for the first time, at an informal summit in Dublin on Friday. The informal format suits the subject. With no political statements to adopt at the end, leaders can speak more openly.

“The President had already thought of putting this discussion on the agenda of the European Council. It’s not always easy. Sometimes it gets overcrowded by current events,” an EU official said, asking not to be named.

That is precisely what has unfolded. The summit was meant to focus on AI, but the question of who should speak for the EU in the Ukraine talks has taken over.

Peace envoy

Ukraine reached the agenda after Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote to Costa warning that the multiple formats in which the EU is engaging in the talks made it “less credible”. She called for a clear mandate to take part in the negotiations.

Costa agreed to add the item and appeared to put himself forward for the job, noting that “the European Union’s interests need to be represented by its institutions, in accordance with the Treaties.”

He already has support. Luxembourg’s Prime Minister Luc Frieden told reporters on Thursday that Costa would be the natural choice as common EU representative.

“We, as heads of government, have a representative. And that is President Costa. We elected him. He is the President of the European Council. I could live with someone else as well, but of course, we have a President,” Frieden said.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas argues that the EU treaties are clear: on European security, she and Costa should be in the driving seat.

“The leaders, of course, may choose differently and go into these discussions again, which is always difficult. Or we should just stick to the agreements that we made in 2024,” she said, pointing to the allocation of the EU’s top jobs that year.

Controversy ahead

The matter is pressing because Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged Europeans to decide who will represent them at the negotiating table by the end of the month.

“It is important to have a discussion about who will represent Europe during these negotiations. That being said, for me the substance is the most important thing. I think we need to stand firm. I think we have to stand united,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said.

Frederiksen and her Swedish counterpart, Ulf Kristersson, had previously criticised the leaders of Norway and Finland for holding direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin without prior consultation.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, meanwhile, defended the E3 format, in which Germany, France and the UK are committed to providing the security guarantees needed to enforce any peace agreement with Russia.

“We will also discuss who, if necessary, will represent the European Union. But that is a matter we will discuss behind closed doors. So, first of all, we have a tried-and-tested format in the E3,” he said, adding that the three were also working with Poland and Italy.

Merz may also raise the financing of Ukraine’s war effort. Costa invited him to do so after he openly threatened to veto an EU budget deal without a unanimous solution on the matter, prompting a backlash from several leaders.

Ukraine financing and the EU budget will take centre stage at a special European Council on 26-27 November.

Artificial intelligence

The AI discussion will have two parts. The first, on boosting Europe’s competitiveness and sovereignty, features Arthur Mensch, CEO of Mistral AI, the French start-up taking on American tech giants in large language models.

US and Chinese companies have largely captured the development of the most advanced AI technologies. To strengthen European players, the EU is advancing rules to ensure that public contracts in sensitive use cases go only to European companies.

The second part turns to AI’s impact on society. Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, one of the field’s most renowned figures, will address leaders. He has been among the most prominent voices warning of the technology’s existential risks, estimating a 10% to 20% risk that AI could cause human extinction by escaping human control.

“The guests will help frame these discussions, to allow the leaders to have a common understanding of how these challenges will be tackled,” the EU official continued.

As the travel industry looks ahead to 2027, a flurry of new reports has offered a glimpse of where holidaymakers might be heading over the next 12 months – and what they’ll be looking for when they get there.

From booking platforms to guidebook publishers, everyone seems to have an opinion on which are the “hot” destinations, whether that’s emerging city break favourites, quieter alternatives, or places gearing up for major cultural events.

Europe features heavily in many of the predictions, with Albania, lesser-known Greek islands and smaller cities in Italy, France and Germany among the destinations attracting attention.

At Euronews Travel, our own predictions for 2027 include a rise in popularity in the Spanish cities of Cádiz, Marbella and Málaga, thanks to the total eclipse next August, as well as trips to second cities, like Basel in Switzerland and Cambridge in the UK.

We also think China, which now allows citizens from more countries than ever to visit for up to 30 days visa-free, will be hot in 2027, while lovers of Indonesia will look past busy Bali and visit the likes of Komodo National Park, Lombok and beautiful Raja Ampat.

So, where should you go to in Europe in 2027? Here are the trending destinations according to the experts.

Europe’s trending destinations for 2027

Expedia

Online travel platform Expedia was among those launching a guide on where to go in 2027, and among its 10 must-visit destinations, two were in Europe.

Expedia ranked the top 10 by the year-on-year increase in searches for a spot, and in seventh place was Perugia in Italy with searches up 35% from 2025 to 2026.

Capital of the Umbria region, Perugia is famous for its hilltop city centre, which is packed with historical sites dating back to the 14th century. It’s also well worth a visit to experience its jazz and chocolate festivals, held respectively in July and November.

The other destination in the top 10 was Chichester, in the south of the UK, where searches were up 30%. The historic city in West Sussex is known for its Roman ruins and is surrounded by city walls, which make up a trail circuit that is the most intact of Roman town defences in southern England.

Chichester is also right on the doorstep of the beautiful South Downs National Park, majestic Arundel Castle and popular beaches, including sandy West Wittering.

Booking.com

Accommodation booking platform Booking.com revealed its 10 trending destinations for 2027, including three in Europe. These are Reims in France, Bratislava in Slovakia, and Pescara in Italy.

Reims, in the heart of France’s Champagne region, is known for its historic cathedral, where French kings were crowned for hundreds of years, as well as the famous Champagne houses whose cellars lie beneath the city. Less than 45 minutes from Paris by high-speed train, it also makes for an easy city break.

Bratislava, Slovakia’s compact capital, sits on the Danube between Vienna and Budapest, with a medieval old town, hilltop castle and lively food and drink scene. Beyond the city, the nearby Little Carpathians are home to vineyards and wine-producing towns.

Pescara, on Italy’s Adriatic coast, is often overlooked in favour of the country’s more famous western coastline, but the city has long sandy beaches, a lively waterfront and plenty of seafood restaurants.

It’s also a good base for exploring the wider Abruzzo region, known for its mountains, national parks and wine.

Lonely Planet

Guidebook publisher Lonely Planet unveiled 25 destinations for its 2027 Best in Travel list, using the knowledge of travel experts based around the globe. Five of the picks are in Europe.

First up is the Veneto region of Italy, home to enormously popular – and overtouristed – Venice. In its guide, Lonely Planet recommends visiting the wider region, from the Dolomites and Lake Garda to cities including historical Verona and Padua.

Šibenik in Croatia, one of the country’s oldest cities, also makes the list. Lonely Planet says it boasts “impressive architecture, gastronomic delights and a colourful calendar of festivals throughout the year”.

While parts of Spain are also hugely overtouristed, León in the north of the country makes an excellent alternative to more popular spots.

The medieval city, on the French Way of the Camino de Santiago, draws in tourists looking to see its gorgeous Gothic architecture and Antoni Gaudí’s Casa Botines.

Coolcations are set to become ever more popular in 2027, so it’s little surprise that Skanör-Falsterbo, the twin towns found in Sweden’s Skåne province, are on this list.

The area, known as the Swedish Riviera, encourages visitors to slow down and soak in the coastal scenery and explore the area’s nature reserves, all while experiencing lower temperatures than much of Europe.

Lonely Planet’s final pick is Dessau in Germany, a city which it says is “synonymous with the Bauhaus movement” and one which packs a big cultural punch despite its small size.

Skyscanner

As part of its wider trends list, travel search engine Skyscanner revealed its top 10 trending destinations for 2027, based on the biggest year-on-year rises in searches on its platform, with four European destinations making the list.

Malmö, in southern Sweden, is known for its mix of historic architecture and modern design, as well as its lively food scene. Its location also makes it an easy base for exploring the wider, cross-border Öresund region, with Copenhagen just a short train ride across the bridge.

Trapani, on Sicily’s western coast, offers a taste of traditional Italian island life, with a historic old town, seafood restaurants and salt pans stretching along the coast. It is also a handy starting point for trips to the Egadi Islands and the hilltop medieval town of Erice.

Meanwhile, the Greek island of Samos is known for its clear-water beaches, ancient sites and green, mountainous interior. It’s also far quieter than some of Greece’s better-known holiday islands, with traditional villages and vineyards adding to its appeal.

Finally, Kittilä, in Finnish Lapland, is a gateway to the region’s winter landscapes. Visitors can head out in search of the Northern Lights, try husky sledding and snowmobiling, or explore nearby ski resorts like Levi, the largest in the country.

Intrepid Travel's Not Hot List

Adventure travel company Intrepid Travel publishes an annual ‘Not Hot List’, highlighting under-the-radar destinations where tourism spending could make a real difference. Three of its 10 picks are in Europe.

Alonnisos, in Greece’s Northern Sporades, offers a quieter alternative to the country’s busier islands, with picturesque villages, beaches and excellent diving. It is home to Europe’s largest marine protected area and Greece’s first underwater museum, at the Peristera shipwreck.

Latvia’s Liepāja is another destination to watch, having been named a European Capital of Culture for 2027. More than 500 cultural events are planned, while its eight-kilometre beach makes it an appealing alternative to the Mediterranean for a summer escape.

Dalsland in Sweden is often dubbed the country’s Lake District. With more than 2,000 lakes and 850 kilometres of gravel-biking routes, it is a haven for outdoor enthusiasts and remains relatively undiscovered. Luckily, it’s becoming more easily accessible thanks to the recent launch of a new rail link between Malmö and Oslo.

National Geographic

National Geographic unveiled its 25 must-visit destinations for 2027, with six European spots making the grade. Its annual "Best of the World" list highlights places offering everything from outdoor adventures to cultural experiences and historic sights.

Its picks are ideal for travellers who have “a sense of adventure, a fascination with the past”, or are seeking the “simple pleasure of wandering unfamiliar city streets”.

Among the trending destinations is Norway’s Vestland, where dramatic fjords, towering cliffs and waterfalls provide the backdrop for adventure and wellness breaks. Poland’s Tricity – comprising Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot – also features, alongside Leipzig in Germany, which is expanding its Music Trail with a new 7.2km loop.

France’s Normandy will mark 1,000 years since William the Conqueror’s birth with more than 1,000 events, while Spain’s Santander is set to welcome two major art museums. Scotland’s Dumfries and Galloway completes the European selection, with a new dark sky observatory due to open next summer.

Advantage Travel Partnership

UK-based travel consortium Advantage Travel Partnership named Albania as a destination to watch for 2027, with its beaches and relatively good value helping to drive interest. The country is increasingly attracting holidaymakers looking beyond Europe’s more established summer hotspots.

The organisation’s booking data also revealed that Spain remained the most popular short-haul choice for British travellers in summer 2026, with Tenerife, Mallorca and the Costa Blanca leading the way – and that’s likely to continue into next year.

Looking ahead, major sporting events including the Ryder Cup in Ireland and the Men’s Rugby World Cup in Australia are expected to influence travel plans in 2027.

Fora Travel

Fora Travel's 2027 Hot List features 10 destinations, including three from Europe: Malta, Slovenia and Finland. According to the travel agency’s global data, bookings for all three nations have seen "significant growth" for next year, with Malta up 129%, Slovenia 152% and Finland 138%.

Malta was highlighted for Valletta’s Baroque streets and medieval walled city of Mdina, which visitors can explore before “heading to the coast”. Slovenia offers a “different way to see more in one trip”, with hikes in the Julian Alps, a few days on Lake Bled and a stop in the vineyards of Goriška Brda. Meanwhile, travellers going to Finland can enjoy “long summer evenings by the lake” and winter stays in Finnish Lapland, where “new glass igloo properties are adding more ways to experience the Northern Lights”.

Virtuoso

According to the Virtuoso Luxe Report, Greece was named the world’s most popular honeymoon destination for 2027, ahead of traditional spots like Bali and the Maldives. Italy came fourth and France eighth, putting three European countries in the top 10.

While iconic cities such as Rome, Florence and Paris remain popular, affluent couples are increasingly looking for quieter alternatives, from Ischia and Puglia to Provence, Burgundy and the Dolomites.

Nigerian media have reported that EU officials in Abuja pledged €100 million in funding, but the European Commission insists the deal is not “a transactional exchange of concessions.”

Details of the EU's “milestone” migration deal with Nigeria remain unclear, two days after it was signed in Abuja by EU Commissioner Magnus Brunner and Nigeria's Foreign Affairs Minister, Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu.

After a decade of negotiations, Nigeria agreed on Tuesday to readmit its nationals residing illegally in European countries, as the EU seeks to speed up the return of irregular migrants.

The agreement establishes “rapid and effective procedures” for returning Nigerians who have no right to stay in an EU country, a pressing issue for the bloc, since only one in three irregular migrants is actually sent back.

Accounts vary over what Nigeria secured in return for the agreement.

According to local press, the EU pledged almost €100 million in additional funding for migration management and security cooperation.

The Nigerian newspaper The Sun, in a report shared on X by the EU delegation in Abuja, attributed the pledge to Johannes Luchner, deputy director general of the Commission’s department for Migration and Home Affairs.

According to these reports, the money would finance legal migration pathways for Nigerians into the EU, as well as anti-trafficking and anti-drug initiatives.

The Commission maintains that the agreement is not “a transactional exchange of concessions.”

“It is part of a broader mutually beneficial partnership between the EU and Nigeria. [...] This is one important step in strengthening our partnership, which is based on mutual trust, shared responsibilities, reciprocity, and common interests,” a Commission spokesperson said on Thursday in response to a question from Euronews.

In a statement, Brunner offered little detail on the agreement, saying only that the EU and Nigeria were “turning the huge potential of [their] partnership into mutual benefit.”

Nigeria's Foreign Affairs Minister and the EU Delegation to Nigeria have yet to respond to Euronews' requests for comment.

The EU has already committed €731 million in grant funding to Nigeria for 2021-2027.

Many Nigerian migrants reach Europe through the dangerous Mediterranean route. Nigerians were the largest national group among irregular arrivals in Italy in 2017 and 2018, but their numbers have dropped significantly since then. Eurostat does not publish figures on the current number of Nigerians residing irregularly in the EU countries.

The agreement is part of a broader effort to raise the share of migrants who are effectively returned after an order to leave. That rate remains around 30%, despite a slight increase in recent months.

Under international law, countries are obliged to readmit their own nationals. However, African governments have often resisted such returns or delayed the process.

To step up cooperation with third countries, the EU is using incentives and leverage across sectors, including visa policy, trade and financial support. Foreign governments, for their part, ask in exchange for substantial visa facilitation or large financial packages.

The EU currently has 18 readmission agreements, most of them with Asian and Western Balkan countries. A 2014 agreement with Cape Verde was the bloc's first with an African nation, but subsequent negotiations with Morocco and Tunisia have stalled.

Some EU member states have negotiated bilateral agreements to return irregular migrants residing on their territory. The EU as a whole has increasingly turned to non-binding arrangements, such as those with Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Ethiopia, or to broader strategic partnerships, such as the memoranda of understanding signed with Tunisia and Egypt.

Under this deal, EU nationals who lack the legal right to remain in Nigeria can also be returned. The agreement still needs approval from EU member states and the European Parliament.

As Europe prepares for the threat of wider conflict, its hospitals and healthcare systems are emerging as a critical — but still underprepared — line of defence.

As Europe braces for the possibility of a wider conflict, governments are pouring money into defence, strengthening NATO's eastern flank and preparing their militaries for a more dangerous security environment.

But there is another frontline that risks being overlooked: Europe's health sector; its hospitals, healthcare workers and public health systems.

From missile and drone attacks to chemical, biological and radiological threats, a major conflict could put healthcare systems under unprecedented pressure.

And with artificial intelligence opening up new possibilities — and risks — in biotechnology, the threats facing Europe are becoming harder to predict.

A prepared healthcare system is not just a matter of public health. It is also a matter of national security, according to Brigadier General Petter Iversen, Norway's Surgeon General and chair of NATO's Committee of the Chiefs of Military Medical Services.

“Healthy society, it's a resilient society,” Iversen told Euronews. “If you are resilient, you can withstand the pressure from the adversaries.”

That means preparing for more than the immediate consequences of a military attack. It means ensuring hospitals can cope with mass casualties, that medical supplies remain available, that healthcare workers know how to operate in extraordinary circumstances and that countries can adapt when several emergencies strike simultaneously.

The new biological threat

One of the biggest uncertainties comes from the rapid development of artificial intelligence and its potential use in biological research.

While AI offers enormous opportunities to accelerate the development of medicines and treatments, it could also make it easier for malicious actors to develop dangerous biological agents.

“You don't know what you are facing, because it can be a virus engineered with AI or a state actor developing a new virus,” Laurent Muschel, Director and Deputy Head of the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA), told Euronews, adding that “biosecurity is going to be very high on the agenda”.

“We need to have the appropriate regulatory framework, the appropriate surveillance system to control the use of AI,” Muschel said. “It's a fantastic technology to develop new medicines, but it can also help bad actors to develop very powerful tools.”

Iversen says a combination of new synthetic biology, new bioinformatics and new techniques for biological development combined with artificial intelligence is taken “really seriously,” with the prospect of weapons of mass destruction remaining among the gravest concerns.

“The horrific thought of the use of weapons of mass destruction and the health implications that will have, both on the chemical and nuclear and biological side, will be the biggest threat,” he said.

Such an attack could generate enormous numbers of patients requiring very different forms of treatment — a combination that would put extraordinary pressure on healthcare capacity.

HERA is working on ways to ensure that medical countermeasures can be deployed against a range of potential threats, including mass-casualty events, bioterrorism and chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats.

One approach is the development of broad-spectrum treatments that could offer protection before the precise nature of a biological threat is known.

“First, broad-spectrum antivirals, broad-spectrum antibodies, monoclonal antibodies. That protects you from the threat, and then targeted treatment,” Muschel said.

Europe is not equally prepared

Governments are increasingly aware that healthcare systems must be ready for these scenarios. But awareness does not necessarily translate into preparedness.

Iversen says countries still need to secure funding, invest in training and regularly exercise their ability to respond.

“We are around 200 metres in the 400-metre lap,” Iversen said. “We are preparing for the finish, and we need to look at how we can use the resources and capabilities, both civilian and military.”

Frontrunners are countries bordering Russia and those on NATO's eastern flank.

“It's natural that the countries bordering Russia and on the eastern flank of Europe have another situational awareness than people further west,” Iversen said.

He pointed to efforts in Germany, Norway and the Baltic and Nordic countries to increase hospital beds and expand healthcare provision.

But infrastructure alone will not be enough.

Iversen warned that preparedness also requires a change in how healthcare systems operate, including training medical professionals to work in unfamiliar conditions.

In peacetime, highly specialised services are essential. But during a war or major crisis, healthcare systems may need to adopt a more generalised approach, allowing staff and facilities to respond flexibly to a sudden influx of patients.

The second vulnerability, he sees, is the supply chain.

“We need a combination of both stockpiling and warehouses, but also an increased industrial base,” to withstand the first wave of a crisis while retaining the capacity to adapt to what comes next, Iversen said.

Ukraine's warning to Europe

For European health authorities, the war in Ukraine has turned many of these scenarios from theoretical exercises into practical lessons.

Hospitals and ambulances have come under attack. Medical workers have had to operate in increasingly dangerous conditions. And the conflict has generated healthcare needs that extend far beyond emergency treatment on the battlefield.

The experience has exposed the importance of trauma care, rehabilitation and mental health services.

“We saw that there is much more need for trauma care,” former Head of WHO Country Office in Ukraine, Jarno Habicht, told Euronews.

The scale of injuries has also created a growing need for rehabilitation, particularly for people who have undergone amputations.

“We have many thousands more amputations that we would not have without war,” Habicht said.

Mental health is another major challenge, both for the wider population and for healthcare workers operating under sustained pressure.

Habicht encouraged leaders to look beyond hospital buildings and equipment to the people who keep healthcare systems running: doctors, nurses, technicians and support staff.

“You need a good building, you need a safe space. But ultimately, you depend on whether the nurses are there, whether the doctors are there, whether the support staff are there,” he said.

Healthcare workers also need the right tools, training and financing to remain in the profession and respond when emergencies hit.

“That's very, very important to realise that healthcare is really part of that whole security and defence system,” Habicht said.

UPDATE sâmbătă, ora 11:30. Microsoft a transmis, în această dimineață, că serviciile sale au fost complet restabilite. Conform BBC, au avut loc întreruperi în 70 de țări ale aplicațiilor și softurilor folosite, la nivel global, de peste 430 de milioane de utilizatori.

UPDATE, vineri, ora 18:25. Conducerea Microsoft a transmis clienților afectați că întreruperea globală de astăzi a fost rezultatul unei “probleme tehnice” și a reiterat că aceasta nu a avut legătură cu un atac cibernetic sau cu agenți de inteligență artificială. “Cu câteva luni în urmă, am actualizat gateway-urile (o poartă către o altă rețea – n.r.) pentru a crește capacitatea, iar această actualizare a introdus o eroare”, se menționează în mesajul trimis clienților.

“Această eroare nu a cauzat nicio problemă cunoscută în ultimele câteva luni. Ieri, a avut loc o modificare a rețelei care a declanșat defecțiuni și a crescut încărcarea asupra unui sistem care, în rest, funcționa corect, provocând o defecțiune în cascadă, a transmis Microsoft.

În prezent, eroarea de bază a fost remediată, însă din cauza volumului mare de operațiuni aflate în așteptare, este restabilită treptat conexiunea pentru clienți și regiuni.

Universitățile și alte instituții de învățământ din Marea Britanie au anunțat că accesul la e-mail și serviciile conexe pare că au revenit la normal în această după-amiază. Între timp, Office for Students, autoritatea de reglementare a învățământului superior din Anglia, a declarat că accesul la e-mail a fost restabilit.

Universitatea din Manchester a comunicat personalului și studenților: “Microsoft a anunțat că se înregistrează progrese încurajatoare în ceea ce privește restabilirea serviciilor în Europa, disponibilitatea serviciilor și performanța livrării e-mailurilor îmbunătățindu-se. Știrea, în forma inițială. Probleme de conectare la serviciile Microsoft Outlook, Teams și 365, la nivel global, puse de companie pe seama unei sarcini ridicate asupra infrastructurii. Multiple raportări au venit și din România în două valuri, aseară și azi-dimineață.

Charles Lamanna, unul dintre directorii companiei, a precizat că nu este vorba despre un incident de securitate cibernetică. Mai devreme, Microsoft a pus situația pe seama “unei sarcini ridicate asupra infrastructurii în mai multe regiuni” – un număr de servere au devenit indisponibile în mod neașteptat – și a transmis că procesul de remediere este mai dificil decât era de așteptat.

În România, primele raportări pe platforma Downdetector în privința serviciului Outlook au fost făcute seara trecută, înaintea orei 20. Un nou val de sesizări se înregistrează în această dimineață. Raportări pe platformă au venit din 74 de țări în decurs de doar o oră, potrivit unei sinteze a BBC. Singapore, Australia, Hong Kong, Japonia sau Filipine au anunțat deja că activitatea școlilor, instanțelor sau băncilor, după caz, este afectată.

OpenAI și Anthropic au informat și ele că unele instrumente furnizate de Microsoft nu funcționează corespunzător, cea din urmă indicând în mod specific suita 365.

Președintele Ucrainei a salutat angajamentul emisarilor americani, Jared Kushner și Steve Witkoff, de a include delegați din partea Uniunii Europene în următoarea rundă de discuții de pace cu Rusia. Decizia vine în contextul în care liderii europeni și-au exprimat, în această săptămână, îngrijorări tot mai mari legate de securitate, iar Volodimir Zelenski a declarat că implicarea lor în discuții ar asigura Uniunii Europene o ”voce” în cadrul negocierilor.

Kushner și Witkoff s-au întâlnit cu Zelenski la Dublin, joi seara, în cadrul unei zile intense de diplomație de tip ”shuttle” (deplasări între părțile implicate). Anterior, aceștia avuseseră o întrevedere la Moscova cu Vladimir Putin, care a precizat că poziția Rusiei față de război – inclusiv solicitările sale teritoriale – a rămas neschimbată.

Aceste întâlniri survin după discuțiile de la Abu Dhabi, care nu au reușit să aducă un progres semnificativ pentru încheierea războiului. Totuși, Rusia și Ucraina au convenit asupra unui nou schimb de prizonieri – cel mai amplu de la lansarea invaziei ruse la scară largă, în 2022. Kushner a afirmat că acest demers va permite întoarcerea a ”mii de oameni la familiile lor”, însă nu au fost oferite detalii suplimentare, precum numărul exact al prizonierilor care vor face obiectul schimbului sau un calendar al acestuia.

Joi, Kushner a declarat că, în ultimele luni, SUA au ”colaborat foarte, foarte strâns cu europenii, lucru care, consider eu, a fost extrem de important”. El a adăugat că i-a subliniat lui Putin cât de important este ca delegații europeni să fie prezenți „la masa negocierilor”. ”Este dispus să încerce”, a completat Kushner. De câțiva ani, Zelenski pledează pentru includerea delegaților europeni în discuțiile de pace, argumentând că acest lucru este logic, având în vedere ambiția pe termen lung a Kievului de a adera la Uniunea Europeană.

Ucraina și statele europene și-au exprimat, de multă vreme, îngrijorarea cu privire la angajamentul actualei administrații americane față de securitatea Europei, precum și față de atitudinea mai conciliantă a acesteia față de Kremlin. Moscova a tratat cu reticență implicarea europenilor, deși aceștia din urmă susțin de mult timp că joacă un rol central în orice dinamică postbelică pe continentul lor.

Joi, Kaja Kallas, vicepreședinte al Comisiei Europene și șefa diplomației UE, a declarat că prezența unui delegat european a demonstrat că, la Kremlin, ”s-a înțeles acum că Europa este un actor important”. De asemenea, Kallas și-a exprimat îndoiala cu privire la existența vreunei intenții reale din partea Rusiei de a avansa spre un acord de pace.

Prim-ministrul irlandez Micheál Martin le-a transmis liderilor europeni reuniți joi în capitala Irlandei că, în opinia sa, securitatea regiunii a fost ”reconfigurată fundamental” de războiul declanșat de Rusia. ”Multe state membre [ale UE] resimt o amenințare existențială din cauza evenimentelor din Ucraina și a riscului — în eventualitatea în care Ucraina ar cădea — ca agresiunea să se extindă pe continentul european”, a declarat el în fața jurnaliștilor.

Chris Van Hollen, who has support from some of the more vocal progressives within the Democratic party, is the first to openly challenge long-term Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer's bid.

US Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate Majority Leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.

The announcement from the progressive senator sets up an internal party clash as long-term Democratic Senate leader Schumer, 75, has faced calls from some in his party to step aside for new leadership.

Van Hollen, who has support from some of the more vocal progressives within the party, is the first senator to openly challenge Schumer.

Van Hollen said in a statement that he is running because “the American people called for change”.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said. “This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Left-wing independent Senator Bernie Sanders said this week that he would not support Schumer in continuing his role.

Newly-elected Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan posted on X that he also backed Van Hollen.

Schumer said he welcomed discussion about the future of the party, but insisted: "I have the votes to continue serving as the Democratic Leader."

"I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people," he wrote on X.

While Schumer is the favorite to win, Van Hollen’s run exposes a rift in the party that opened in the spring of 2025, when Schumer was put on the defensive since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote.

Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.

Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.

It will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades. The question of whether to reelect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote.
